notes.meaning: God tells Ezekiel to sing a funeral song for the wealthy city of Tyre. Even though Tyre brought trouble on herself through sin, God's prophet is told to mourn her tragic fall. This shows that we should feel sorrow over the ruin of other people and nations.

God speaks directly to Tyre, which sat at the entrance of the sea with its busy ports. Tyre was filled with pride, boasting that it was flawless in beauty. It trusted in its wealth and worldly fame rather than in the Lord.

The prophet begins describing Tyre as if it were a splendid sailing ship. The city was built on an island surrounded by the sea, and its builders designed every part with great skill. Its human builders made it look glorious, but its beauty was purely worldly.

The builders used the best cypress from Mount Senir to construct the ship's wooden sides. They brought tall, strong cedars from Lebanon to serve as its mast. Tyre gathered the finest timber from surrounding lands to display its power.

The oars were crafted from sturdy oak trees from Bashan. The deck was made of fine wood inlaid with expensive ivory brought from the coasts of Cyprus. Tyre spared no expense to make its vessel luxurious and magnificent.

The sail was made of fine embroidered linen from Egypt and served as a proud banner for all to see. Colorful purple cloth from the shores of Greece was stretched over the deck as an awning to give shade. Everything about the ship showed off Tyre's wealth and self-confidence.

Men from neighboring coastal cities like Sidon and Arvad served as rowers at the oars. But Tyre kept the top leadership roles for herself, choosing her own skilled men to be captains and navigators. This showed how Tyre ruled over surrounding towns and used them for its own gain.

Experienced craftsmen from the city of Gebal were brought on board to plug leaks and keep the ship watertight. Ships and sailors from all over the world docked alongside Tyre to trade in its busy market. Every maritime people contributed to the city's vast commercial engine.

Tyre hired foreign soldiers from distant lands like Persia, Lydia, and Put to serve in its army. These warriors hung their shields and helmets on the city walls during peacetime. Their military presence gave the city a reputation of great splendor and security.

Local men from Arvad and skilled guards stood watch around the walls and upon the towers. Their hung shields completed the look of an invincible, perfectly fortified fortress. Tyre believed its defenses made it completely safe from any enemy attack.

Tarshish in distant Spain traded rich mineral treasures with Tyre. They exchanged silver, iron, tin, and lead for Tyrian goods. Tyre gathered essential metals from the far reaches of the known world to grow even richer.

Peoples from Greece and the regions near the Black Sea brought bronze goods and human slaves to trade. They bought and sold human lives for economic profit alongside everyday wares. This trade in people directly violated the dignity that God gave to all humanity.

The people of Beth-togarmah, from the mountains of Armenia, brought work horses, war horses, and mules to Tyre's markets. They traded these animals in exchange for Tyre's manufactured goods. This gave Tyre powerful beasts for transport and warfare.

Merchants from Dedan along the Persian Gulf brought exotic goods to Tyre. They paid for Tyrian goods with precious ebony wood and elephant tusks. These luxury items fed the city's appetite for outward elegance.

Aram, or Syria, traded fine cloth, embroidery, and sparkling jewels like rubies and coral for Tyre's products. Tyre's own craftsmen produced goods that attracted high-end items from neighboring nations. The city became a center for the most expensive decorative goods.

Judah and Israel also traded with Tyre, but they brought useful agricultural goods rather than mere luxuries. They exchanged excellent wheat, honey, olive oil, and medicinal balm for Tyrian goods. God provided his chosen people with healthy staples that sustained life, which even wealthy Tyre needed to survive.

Damascus traded with Tyre because of the vast wealth and products the city offered. They brought sweet wine from Helbon and fine white wool. This showed how Tyre drew the most prized goods from its neighbors.

Traders from southern Arabia brought well-crafted iron, along with sweet spices like cassia and cane, for Tyre's goods. These traders traveled back and forth to bring raw materials and spices to Tyre's markets. God provided different gifts to different regions so nations could trade to help one another.
Another group of traders from Dedan provided rich saddlecloths and blankets for riding horses and chariots. These expensive coverings added to the comfort and luxury of Tyre's elite.

The desert tribes of Arabia, including the rulers of Kedar, brought animals from their vast herds. They traded lambs, rams, and goats in Tyre's markets. This steady supply of livestock provided food and offerings for the city.

Merchants from Sheba and Raamah in Arabia brought gold, precious gems, and the very best spices. Caravans crossed long distances to bring these costly treasures to Tyre. The city was the ultimate destination for the world's most valuable riches.

Traders from ancient cities across Mesopotamia, such as Haran and Eden, did business with Tyre. Merchants from Sheba and neighboring regions traveled along major caravan routes to meet there. Tyre's markets connected the Mediterranean world to the great river lands of the east.

These Mesopotamian merchants brought beautiful blue robes, skilled embroidery, and colorful rugs tightly wrapped with cords. Many of these precious goods were stored in cedar boxes to keep them safe and fresh. Tyre's markets were filled with the most elaborate and luxurious clothing of the ancient world.

Large sea-going trading ships, known as ships of Tarshish, carried Tyre's merchandise across the seas. The city was packed like a vessel loaded down with heavy cargo in the middle of the waters. Tyre appeared completely secure and glorious in its wealth.

The poem suddenly shifts to the tragic wreck of this magnificent ship. Tyre's own leaders and advisers rowed the city into dangerous, stormy waters through foolish choices and pride. God used King Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian army, like a violent east wind, to shatter the city in the sea.

When the ship breaks apart, all its vast wealth, trade goods, sailors, pilots, repairmen, and hired soldiers sink into the ocean. Everything the city relied on disappears in a single day of catastrophe. Trusting in created things rather than the living God always leads to total ruin.

The terrifying screams of Tyre's dying captains and sailors echo across the water. The shock of their desperate cries causes the surrounding coasts and mainland settlements to tremble with dread. The noise of sudden disaster replaces the bustle of prosperous trade.

Sailors and ship captains from other fleets abandon their vessels in sheer panic and rush to the shore. Seeing the greatest maritime city collapse makes them realize their own ships cannot save them. They stand on solid ground, stunned by the loss of the world's greatest merchant center.

From the shore, the watching sailors cry out loudly and bitterly over Tyre's destruction. They throw dust on their heads and sit in ashes as signs of deep grief. The sight of such enormous power vanishing leaves them brokenhearted and afraid.

The mourners shave their heads bald and put on rough sackcloth instead of fine linen. They weep with deep inner anguish over the complete ruin of their trading partner. All joy and singing are replaced by bitter weeping.

As they grieve, they compose a funeral song asking who was ever as great as Tyre, and who has ever been silenced so completely. What was once the most vibrant city on earth has now become still as the grave. The sea that used to protect Tyre has become its tomb.

The lament looks back on Tyre's past glory, remembering how its sea cargo once satisfied the desires of many nations. Its trade enriched earthly kings through valuable wares and steady tax income. The whole ancient economy had thrived because Tyre was open for business.

Now the magnificent ship is wrecked, broken by the surging waves and dragged down into deep water. All the traded goods and every person on board have drowned together. Human greatness and riches cannot withstand the judgment of God.

The people living along distant coastlines and islands are frozen in horror at the news of Tyre's fall. Foreign kings tremble with fear, unable to hide the panic showing on their faces. They realize that if mighty Tyre can be destroyed, their own kingdoms are in grave danger too.

Merchants from other nations gasp or hiss in shock and mockery at Tyre's sudden disaster. The city has become a terrifying warning to the whole world and will never rise again. This tragic end reminds everyone that earthly glory without God is fragile and temporary.
